meta.title: Beta-Binomial model
reference.title: Further reading
reference.text: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2013, chapters 1–2.
content.0: Suppose $X$ is the number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with success probability $p$.
content.2: For observed $x$ successes, the likelihood is proportional to $p^x(1-p)^{n-x}$ as a function of $p$. The Beta prior density is proportional to $p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$, for $\alpha,\beta>0$.

content.9: Its posterior mean is $10/14\approx0.714$, while the observed proportion is $8/10=0.8$. The Beta prior is conjugate to the Binomial likelihood because the posterior is also a Beta distribution.
content.11: Compare the prior with the posterior. Change the observed counts to see how new data affect the distribution.
content.12:
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)
plot(p, dbeta(p, 2, 2), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Probability of success", ylab = "Density")
lines(p, dbeta(p, 10, 4), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Prior", "Posterior"),
       col = c("black", "steelblue"), lwd = 2)
